ch05.title: The First Preaching Tour
ch05.b002: It was the first day of the week, Sunday, January 19, A.D. 27, exactly seven days after the ordination. From early morning the yard of Zebedee’s house in Bethsaida was crowded. The apostles’ wives and children were there, and aged parents, and disciples from Bethsaida and Capernaum, all come to say good-bye. The twelve themselves knew very little. They knew they were going up to Jerusalem for the Passover in April, and that they would travel by way of the Jordan valley. Beyond that, the plan lived only in the Master’s mind.
ch05.b003: Peter stood between his wife and his three children and said the same things over and over. He would be back soon after the Passover. They were to mind their grandmother. The youngest would not let go of the hem of his cloak. Peter swung the child up into the air, set him down again, and laughed loudly—so loudly that the laugh seemed to be covering something. His wife said nothing. She retied the cord of his bundle with careful fingers. She did not fully understand what her husband was setting out to do, but she knew this man well enough to know that once he had set his heart on a thing, he did not turn back. The farewells went on and on, and it was near noon before the company was ready to leave.
ch05.b004: Then someone said that the Master was missing. Andrew went to look for him. John watched him go from the far end of the yard and, without quite meaning to, let his eyes travel once more over the faces around him. John was the one who handled the affairs of the Master’s family. He knew them all: the brothers in Nazareth, the married sisters, Mary the mother, growing old. He knew those faces better than anyone. And only now did he notice that among all these faces not one of theirs was to be found. Something in his chest went cold.
ch05.b005: A little later Andrew came up from the shore with the Master beside him, and Andrew’s face was strangely set. John heard the story afterward. Andrew had found Jesus sitting alone in a boat drawn up along the beach, and he was weeping. The twelve had often seen their Master grieve; they had seen him lost in grave thought. But none of them had ever seen him weep. Andrew had gone to him and asked why, on so great a day, when they were setting out to proclaim the kingdom, he should be in tears. Had one of them given offense? Walking back with Andrew, Jesus told him that none of them had grieved him. He was sad only because no one of his father Joseph’s family had remembered to come and wish them Godspeed.
ch05.b006: John held on to those words for a long time. Ruth, the youngest sister, happened to be away visiting her brother Joseph in Nazareth. But the others had simply not come—kept away by pride, by disappointment, by misunderstanding, by small resentments nursed over hurt feelings. John knew each of the reasons, and that made it worse. This man, who wandered without a house of his own, had taken painstaking care to provide for his mother and his brothers and sisters, and John himself had helped him do it. Yet today that family was not in the yard. John remembered what he had heard on the highland the week before: whoever would be first must be the one who serves. He felt suddenly ashamed of the quiet pride he had taken in being one of the three who stood closest to the Master. To stand beside this man, he thought, was not an honor first. It meant standing beside his loneliness.
ch05.b007: The First Camp on the Jordan
ch05.b008: More than a hundred believers wanted to come along, but Jesus earnestly asked them not to follow. They agreed to stay behind, yet within a few days many of them came after him anyway. The first day the company went only as far as Tarichea and spent the night there. It was Thomas’s village. Thomas said little that evening. His house, with his wife and four children in it, lay within easy walking distance, and he slept among the apostles.
ch05.b009: The next day they reached the Jordan near Pella, the very bank where John had preached about a year before and where Jesus had been baptized. The winter river ran muddy, and birds flew low over the reed beds. They stayed there more than two weeks. Before the first week was out, several hundred people had gathered in a camp around them, from Galilee and Phoenicia, from Syria and the Decapolis, from Perea and Judea.
ch05.b010: Jesus did no public preaching. Andrew divided the crowd and assigned which apostles would preach at the morning and afternoon gatherings. For the first time Peter stood before so many strange faces. His first words stuck in his throat, but from the second sentence on they came freely. As he spoke he could feel the faces leaning toward him, and the feeling was very like the weight in his hands when a net grows heavy. In the evenings, after supper, the Master sat with the twelve, went back over what he had already taught them, and answered their questions. One evening he told them something of the forty days he had spent alone in the hills near that place. The apostles listened without a sound.
ch05.b011: Three out of every four people in the camp had been baptized by John. They wanted to hear the new teacher, but one thing always caught at them. If this man was the one John had announced, why did he do nothing to get John out of prison? They put the question to the apostles, and the apostles had no answer.
ch05.b012: Each time Judas Iscariot heard that question, he felt something strange. It was his own question. On the evening the twelve first gathered at Zebedee’s house, he had taken the Master aside and asked exactly that, and the answer had not satisfied him. Now hundreds were asking the same thing. *I was not wrong,* Judas thought, and he drew a curious comfort from the thought. The comfort did not last. If the question was right, then what was the man who would not answer it? Judas did not follow that thought to its end. Instead, night after night, when Andrew patiently coached his fellow apostles in the delicate art of getting along with John’s disciples, Judas sat at the very back and nodded.
ch05.b013: On the night before they left Pella, the Master spoke to them about the kingdom in a new way. While the Father’s will was only their law, he said, they stood barely at the threshold of the kingdom; when the Father’s will had truly become their own will, then the kingdom was established within them. He was asking them to be, not slaves bowing to a statute, but free sons. Some of them grasped part of it. But the only one who seemed to take hold of the whole was James Zebedee. John saw that his brother’s face that night was unusually still. James said nothing at all. He only sat a long while listening to the sound of the river.
ch05.b015: They moved on to the neighborhood of Amathus and stayed almost three weeks. The apostles preached to the crowds twice every day, and Jesus spoke only on Sabbath afternoons. The old habit of resting on Wednesdays could no longer be kept, so Andrew arranged that two apostles in turn would rest on each of the six working days, while on the Sabbath every man was on duty.
ch05.b016: Most of the public preaching fell to Peter, James, and John. Philip, Nathaniel, Thomas, and Simon did personal work with inquirers who came seeking them out, and the twins kept order among the crowds. Andrew, Matthew, and Judas became a committee of three that managed the whole household. Judas liked the post. Sums and plans and accounts were what he did best. And yet, in the evenings, when the three fishermen came back from preaching with their faces flushed, he would find himself pulling the strings of the money bag a little tighter for no reason. It was always those three who stood before the crowds.
ch05.b017: Andrew was busy every day keeping the peace between John’s disciples and the newer disciples of Jesus. Every few days a serious quarrel broke out. When he could bear it no longer and brought the matter to the Master, the answer was always the same: a host does well not to meddle in the family troubles of his guests, and a wise parent does not take sides in the small quarrels of his children. So Andrew went back with that answer and, with the help of the other apostles, untangled the quarrel himself.
ch05.b018: The subject the Master returned to most often at Amathus was the nature of God. Again and again he told them that God was not some great bookkeeper writing down every sin of his children so as to settle the account against them at the end. He was a Father. When Thomas asked who, then, was the God of this kingdom, Jesus said that God was their Father, and that his gospel was nothing more than the believing recognition that they were God’s sons. At the word *bookkeeper* Judas raised his head. He kept accounts every day. Not a coin went missing; he remembered who had spent how much. That was his greatest virtue. And now he was told that God was not like that. Judas weighed whether this was praise or reproof, and concluded it was neither. God might not count, but men had to, or the thirteen of them would go hungry next week. With that thought he closed his ledger.
ch05.b019: One evening in council James Zebedee asked how they might learn to see things alike, and so live together in greater harmony. The question visibly stirred the Master. John saw it. Jesus spoke his brother’s name twice. Then he asked when he had ever taught them that they must all see alike. He had come, he said, to bring spiritual liberty, so that each person might live an original life of his own before God. Their thinking, their temperaments, their ways of acting could differ as much as they liked. If they shared one motive, the wholehearted doing of the Father’s will, and one goal, the finding of the Father, then they were one.
ch05.b020: John glanced at his brother. James could be fiery one moment and then, for no reason anyone could see, fall silent for days. The two brothers loved each other, but working together had never been easy. John thought he understood why James had asked. And he thought he understood why the answer had seemed to give the Master such joy. What James had really wanted to ask was not how they could all become the same. It was whether men as different as they were could still go on together.
ch05.b021: Near the end of their time at Amathus, Simon Zelotes brought to Jesus a Persian named Teherma, who did business in Damascus. Andrew had handed him over to Simon for instruction, and Simon, taking him for a fire worshiper, argued with him zealously. Teherma would not budge—until he talked with the Master, after which he announced that he would stay several days longer. When Simon and Jesus were alone, Simon asked why the man would not listen to him yet listened so readily to the Master. Jesus told him not to labor to take anything out of a seeking heart, but only to put something into a hungry soul. Bring men into the kingdom, he said, and its living truths would soon drive out the error. Simon was astonished, but he did as he was told, and Teherma entered the kingdom.
ch05.b023: On February 26 they went down the Jordan to the ford near Bethany in Perea, the place where John had first cried out that the kingdom was coming. There they stayed four weeks.
ch05.b024: In the second week the Master took only Peter, James, and John across the river into the hills south of Jericho for three days of rest. On the morning they left, Peter tried hard not to look back. He could feel the eyes of the nine on his back. He did not know that Judas’s eyes rested on him longest of all.
ch05.b025: The hills were dry and still. By day the limestone slopes glared white; by night the stars hung so low it seemed one could reach up and touch them. The Master taught the three of them many things. His religion, he told them, would rest not on books or laws or organizations but on the life he himself was living among men. He had deliberately passed by the great men of the earth and begun his work among the poor. And he had come, he said, not merely to set an example for a few creatures on this earth, but to establish a standard of human life for all peoples on all the worlds of his universe.
ch05.b026: Peter felt a chill run down his spine as he listened. All the worlds? Could it be that the man was not in his right mind? The thought flashed through his head and he shook it off, startled at himself. But when he looked aside, he saw the same shadow passing over the faces of James and John. The three of them met one another’s eyes and quickly looked away. No one spoke the thought aloud. That night Peter lay awake, staring for a long time into the darkness where the Master sat. The man hurried over nothing. Nothing surprised him. That was not the stillness of a madman. Peter knew that much at least.
ch05.b027: James marveled at something else in those three days. The Master seemed to see the end from the beginning. He was never excited, never vexed, never thrown off balance. He never made excuses or apologies to anyone. At times he looked sad, but never discouraged. John noticed something different again. The man was a man. However vast the things he said, at night he pulled his cloak tight against the cold, and in the morning he ate dry bread with relish. He lived as a man among men, and yet he was without fault. John could not understand how both could be true of one person. None of the three understood half of what was said in those three days. But the words sank down inside them, and years later, when each of them had to preach alone, they rose up one by one.
ch05.b028: Since Amathus the Master had been teaching them more fully about caring for the sick. A man is body, mind, and spirit bound together, he said, and so they must learn to tell apart sickness of the flesh, the troubles of a disturbed mind, and what people called possession by evil spirits. The apostles did not grasp all the distinctions, but month by month they gave themselves more to the ministry of healing. During the four weeks at Bethany beyond the Jordan, Andrew sent the apostles up to Jericho in pairs several times each week. They went from house to house and comforted the afflicted. It was there that they first discovered how much comfort the good news of the kingdom brought to the sick. Jericho was the place where the commission to preach the glad tidings and to minister to the afflicted was first fully carried out.
ch05.b030: On the way up to Jerusalem all thirteen stopped in Jericho. They meant to stay a single day, but a company from Mesopotamia, come to confer with the Master, overtook them there, and Jesus spent three days with these men.
ch05.b031: For those three days Judas walked the streets of Jericho. The shade of the palms, the scent of the balsam groves, the noise of the market before the gate. He had been born in Kerioth, but this was the city where he had grown up. Here he had helped in his father’s businesses and learned his figures; here he had first heard the rumor of John the Baptist; and here his Sadducee parents had disowned him when he said he would follow John. At the mouth of a certain lane he stopped, stood a moment, and turned away without going in.
ch05.b032: His Galilean companions found Jericho a wonder. The twins stood with their mouths open, gazing up at the tops of the palms, and Nathaniel pretended to be scandalized at the price of dates. Judas told them about this and that. For the first time he felt that within this company he was the one leading the way. Judea was his country; here the Galilean fishermen were guests. The feeling was warm, and at the same time a little lonely, for everything that had once tied him to this land was cut. All he had left were these Galileans. He knew it, and so he wished they would grow closer to him—no, that they would count him closer to them. He told no one of that wish.
ch05.b033: On Monday, the last day of March, they began the climb up the hills toward Jerusalem. Lazarus of Bethany had already come down to the Jordan twice to see the Master and had arranged everything so that his home could serve as their headquarters. John’s disciples stayed by the river, so only the twelve went with the Master to Lazarus’s house. To Martha and Mary it was a great event to have the Master and his apostles under their brother’s roof. The company rested there five days.
ch05.b034: John remembered those five days for a long time. Martha never left the oven from dawn on; Mary was always heating water to wash the guests’ feet. The fig tree in the courtyard was putting out its first leaves. In the evenings Lazarus went round with a lamp, checking each guest’s bed. The twins offered to carry the household’s water jars and were pushed out of the way by Martha. John laughed as he watched, and then the yard at Bethsaida came back to him—the faces that had not been there that day. And here were people with not a drop of shared blood welcoming the Master as one of their own. It seemed to John that the Master was unusually at ease in this house. Whether that was true, or only how it looked to him, he could not say.
ch05.b035: On Sunday morning, April 6, they went down to Jerusalem. It was the first time the Master and all twelve had entered the city together. As they rounded the slope of the Mount of Olives, the white stone and gold of the temple burst into light all at once in the morning sun. The twins stopped in their tracks; Philip began to reckon something and gave it up. Only Judas did not slow his pace. He had seen this sight many times. Yet today it was as if he were seeing it for the first time. Today he was passing through these gates with a man who might be the Messiah.
ch05.b037: On the first day in Jerusalem the Master called on Annas, the onetime high priest, a friend of former years and a relative of Salome, Zebedee’s wife. He was kin on John’s mother’s side.
ch05.b038: John had heard that name since childhood. His mother took a quiet pride in the fact that her side of the family included a man who had been high priest. John even knew the faces of the doorkeeper and a few of the servants of that house. So when he heard that evening how the visit had ended, his face burned. Annas had received the Master coldly. Seeing it, Jesus had at once taken his leave, saying as he went that fear is the great enslaver of men and pride their great weakness, and asking whether Annas would sell himself into bondage to both. Annas made no reply.
ch05.b039: John pictured the scene: the marble floor, the old priest sitting stiffly upright, and the Galilean carpenter turning quietly away before him. The house his mother had boasted of had opened its door only halfway to his Master. John was ashamed of it, and at the same time he felt a strange release. What was a great family in this world, after all? For the first time, sharing blood with that house gave him no pride at all. The Master did not see Annas again until three years later, on the night when Annas sat with his son-in-law in judgment on the Son of Man. That night the woman who kept the gate would recognize John, and at his request would let Peter into the courtyard. In the courtyard a charcoal fire would be burning. But none of that was yet known to anyone.
ch05.b040: All that month the Master or one of the apostles taught in the temple every day. When the Passover crowds were too great to get in, they held their meetings outside the sacred precincts. Their message was simple: the kingdom of heaven was at hand; by faith in the fatherhood of God anyone could become a son of God; the rule of life in that kingdom was love. Preaching beneath the temple porches, Peter heard his own voice strike the stone columns and come back to him, a sound utterly unlike the wind on the Sea of Galilee. The city frightened him, and he liked being frightened. Rumors reached them that the chief priests and rulers were debating what to do with them, and Peter heard even that as proof that the kingdom was near.
ch05.b041: Judas, in the same courts, heard something else. The Judeans picked out a Galilean accent instantly. Judas did not miss how certain scribes twisted their mouths at the fishermen’s swallowed gutturals. His own speech was like theirs. In the crowd he could pass for a Galilean or for a Judean, and from moment to moment he weighed which side to stand on—and despised himself a little for doing it. But when he saw the crowds pressing in by the hundreds to listen, the scales in him fell quiet. One day a man from Damascus asked how they could know for certain that the Master was sent from God. Jesus asked in return what worthy father would keep his son in anxious doubt about his place in the family, and told him that whoever is born of the spirit carries within himself the power to overcome all doubt. The crowd stayed with him for hours. From that day the apostles too preached with more power. They had never faced such multitudes before, and they learned lessons there that would serve them for years.
ch05.b043: Once or twice a week the Master spent the night in the house of Flavius, a Greek Jew, a proselyte of the gate who had been neither circumcised nor baptized. Flavius had filled his house with statues and works of art gathered from all over the world. At first he feared those images would offend the Master. But Jesus went from room to room admiring each piece and even asking about them. Peter hung back at the doorway, uneasy under the white eyes of the marble figures. Were these not things the law forbade? But the Master saw them as beauty, and asked Flavius why a man should expect rebuke for loving the beauty of what the Father had made and what human hands had fashioned. The next day Flavius went across the Jordan to Bethany and was baptized by John’s disciples.
ch05.b044: In that same house Andrew quietly arranged a meeting between the Master and Jacob, a wealthy trader from Crete. Jacob asked how the jealous, wrathful God of Moses and the prophets could be the same as the merciful Father the Master proclaimed. In the course of their talk Jesus remarked that Jacob, being the father of many, must know the truth of what he said, and Jacob was startled—how did the Master know he had six children? Jesus told him that small children take a father’s punishment for anger alone, but grown children ought to see the love inside it; so should mankind grow up and see God more clearly. Listening, Peter thought of the three children he had left in Bethsaida. The little hand that would not let go of his cloak. He remembered what his own face had looked like when he scolded them, and was silent a long while. Jacob said he believed.
ch05.b045: That night the apostles poured out questions about the Father in heaven. The Master gently chided them for not knowing even the traditions of Israel, and then traced step by step how the idea of God had grown: from the god of the Sinai clans, to the Most High of Melchizedek, to Isaiah’s merciful Creator, and at last to the Father in heaven. He showed them how one record said God had moved David to number the people, while a later record of the same event said it was Satan. The apostles had never been so shaken. They were too bewildered even to ask anything. When he finished, no one put a question, and each went silently to his sleep. That night, for once, even Peter asked nothing.
ch05.b046: One evening Nicodemus, a member of the Sanhedrin, came to see the Master. He was old and wealthy. He had heard Jesus teach in the temple courts, but he was afraid of being seen, and so through Andrew he had asked to meet him privately after dark. When the conversation began, Peter, James, and John were out in Flavius’s garden. Lamplight slipped out between the fig leaves, and low voices drifted through the open window.
ch05.b047: The Master said that unless a man was born from above, he could not see the kingdom of God. Nicodemus asked how an old man could be born again—surely he could not enter his mother’s womb a second time. Just then a night breeze passed through the garden, and all the fig leaves stirred and rustled at once. Through the window the Master’s voice went on. When the wind blows, he said, you hear the rustling of the leaves, but you do not see the wind; you do not know where it comes from or where it goes; so it is with everyone born of the spirit.
ch05.b048: Peter held his breath. The wind that had just gone by was still on the back of his neck. He was a fisherman who had lived his whole life in the wind—the wind that filled a sail, the wind that snarled a net, the wind that could overturn the lake in a single night. He had never once seen it. And he had never once doubted it. He looked at John beside him. John was looking at him. Neither said a word. A little later the three of them went inside to hear the rest. Nicodemus went away deeply moved but bewildered. Watching him go, Peter thought that what so learned a man could not grasp, he himself had perhaps caught a little of just now, on the breath of the wind. The thought made him glad—and a little proud.
ch05.b050: On the Wednesday after Passover week they rested at Bethany. That afternoon Thomas asked a question. On the day of their ordination, he said, they had been taught how they themselves must live, but what were they to teach the people? Might believers own slaves? Should they court poverty and shun property? If mercy alone prevailed, was there to be no more law and justice? The Master talked all afternoon, and after supper on into the night, using the family as his picture. A true father gives his children life, provides for them, trains them, corrects them, stays close to them, forgives them freely, and leaves something behind for the generations to come. All of this, he said, he already knew in perfection in his own relation to the Father.
ch05.b051: But Thomas was still not satisfied. The Father in heaven, he said, did not always seem to deal kindly with them; there was much suffering on earth, and prayers were not always answered. Under the lamp, everyone held his breath. The Master spoke Thomas’s name twice. Then he asked how long it would be before they learned to listen with the ear of the spirit, why they kept translating his words about the spirit into the language of the flesh, how long he must go on speaking to them as children. It was a rebuke. No one in the room could lift his head.
ch05.b052: Yet the Master did not end there. In spite of everything, he said, he loved them. He would bear with them to the very end of their life together in the flesh. And even then his spirit would go before them into all the world.
ch05.b053: Peter felt something break open inside him at those words. Love had come right on the heels of rebuke. He had not known that a promise of patience could sound so warm. He knew how much patience he himself required—a man whose words ran ahead of his thoughts, whose morning resolve was reversed by evening. *To the very end.* He repeated it to himself and then stopped short. The end? When would that be? He thought of the night by the fire when he had sworn that, whatever came, he would never turn back. That oath grew hot in his chest again. Beside him John sat with his head bowed. He was thinking of the tears in the boat: the man abandoned by his own family, weeping, was now promising to bear with disciples who did not understand him, all the way to the end.
ch05.b054: By the end of April the opposition of the Pharisees and Sadducees had become unmistakable. They spent the whole month of May in Bethlehem and Hebron, doing no public preaching, only going from house to house. The people there assumed the Master had been born in Nazareth. The twelve knew he had been born right here in Bethlehem. Peter would sometimes stop short in a narrow lane. Somewhere behind these stone walls that man had cried his first cry. The thought put a strange catch in his throat. For part of that month, while the apostles taught and cared for the sick in the villages, the Master went with Abner to Engedi to visit the Nazarite colony there, the place John the Baptist had come from. Many of them believed in him, but most would not accept him as a teacher sent from heaven because he did not teach fasting and self-denial. In June they returned to Jerusalem and pitched their tents in a shaded park on the western slope of the Mount of Olives, not far from the brook Kidron. People called the place Gethsemane.
ch05.b055: Judas loved that garden. The olive trees were old and bent, but their shade was deep, and in the evenings one could watch the sun go down beyond the city walls. He sat in front of his tent putting his accounts in order and listening to the evening trumpets sounding from inside the city. One Friday evening Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea came out to see the Master. But the two men stood at the entrance of his tent, hesitated a while, and then turned back. They were afraid. Judas watched them disappear into the dark. Even members of the Sanhedrin were afraid to stand beside this man. Judas made a note of it in his mind. If this man really had power, he would not let them turn away like that. The Master knew all about the two men’s coming and going. Judas did not know that.
ch05.b056: Late in June a member of the Sanhedrin named Simon openly took the Master’s side. At once a fresh agitation to arrest Jesus rose up, and the Master decided to withdraw to the cities of Samaria and the Decapolis. On the night before they left, John lay outside the tent and looked up at the stars through the olive branches. A breeze moved the leaves. He remembered what he had heard in the garden of Flavius: a thing you can hear but cannot see. What night this garden would one day hold, he could not have dreamed. That night Gethsemane was only quiet and cool, and the thirteen slept deeply in its keeping.
ch05.b058: The events follow Papers 141 and 142: the departure of January 19, Jesus weeping in the boat, the absence of Joseph’s family and Ruth’s visit to Nazareth (141:0.1–0.2); the believers asked to stay behind, the first night at Tarichea, the camp near Pella with Andrew assigning the preachers, the account of the forty days, and the stumbling stone for John’s followers (141:1.1–1.5); the teaching before leaving Pella, grasped in full only by James Zebedee (141:2.1–2.3); the division of labor and rest days at Amathus, Andrew’s mediation and Jesus’ reply (141:3.1–3.3); the Father who is no bookkeeper, Thomas’s question, and the three forms of affliction (141:4.1–4.9); James’s question on unity (141:5.1–5.3); Simon and Teherma (141:6.1–6.3); Bethany beyond Jordan and the three days with Peter, James, and John (141:7.1–7.15); Jericho, the Mesopotamian delegation, Lazarus’s home and the entry of April 6 (141:8.1–9.3); the visit to Annas (142:0.2); the temple teaching (142:1.1–1.7); Jacob of Crete and that night’s discourse on the growth of the idea of God (142:2.1–3.23); Flavius (142:4.1–4.4); the man from Damascus (142:5.1–5.5); Nicodemus (142:6.1–6.9); Thomas’s questions, the family illustration, the rebuke and the words of love (142:7.1–7.17); Bethlehem and Hebron, the tents at Gethsemane, the two who turned back at the tent door, and Simon of the Sanhedrin (142:8.1–8.5). The link between Annas and John looks ahead to 184:1–2.
ch05.b059: Character facts come from Paper 139: Peter’s wife and three children (139:2.1); John as agent for Jesus’ family and his hidden conceit (139:4.1–4.5, 139:4.9); the silences and balance of James (139:3.3–3.4); Judas’s birthplace, his upbringing in Jericho and his parents’ disowning of him (139:12.1–12.2), and his notion that Jesus was afraid to assert his power (139:12.4); Thomas’s home and family at Tarichea (139:8.2).
ch05.b060: Fiction has been added in the apostles’ inner thoughts and feelings, in weather and landscape, in Peter’s farewell to his family, John’s noticing the absence of Jesus’ family, Judas’s walk through Jericho, the first sight of Jerusalem, the wind in Flavius’s garden (the text gives only Jesus’ figure of speech), and the look between Peter and John. John’s hearing of the Annas visit and his mother’s pride, Judas watching Nicodemus and Joseph turn back, the daily life of the five days at Lazarus’s house, and Peter in the lanes of Bethlehem are also invented. The text says only that the three apostles were tempted to think Jesus might be beside himself; their faces in that moment are imagined.
ch05.b061: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
